title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:genetics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Chromosomal microarray. Genome-wide CNVs and regions of homozygosity; misses balanced rearrangements; first-line for developmental delay, autism, ID.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:genetics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: FISH. Fluorescent probe for a chosen region; fast interphase aneuploidy screening, microdeletions; needs a hypothesis.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:genetics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Karyotype. Low resolution; detects aneuploidies and large rearrangements; needs dividing (metaphase) cells; banding 550-850 bands.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:genetics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: MLPA. Targeted, rapid, cheap test for exon deletions/duplications (DMD, BRCA1, MSH2).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:genetics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Next-generation sequencing. Exome or panels; detects SNVs and indels, some small CNVs; weak for large structural anomalies.
By origin (constitutional vs acquired), distribution (homogeneous vs mosaic), type (numerical: aneuploidy, polyploidy; structural).
Nondisjunction of homologues (meiosis I) or sister chromatids (meiosis II) → gametes n+1 or n−1.
13 Patau (non-viable, cleft, polydactyly), 18 Edwards (~1:5,000, rocker-bottom feet), 21 Down (~1:700, viable, ID, AV canal).
Digyny (diploid egg) and diandry (dispermy or diplospermy).
Balanced: no net gain/loss, normal carrier, unbalanced gametes. Unbalanced: partial trisomy/monosomy.
Terminal and interstitial deletions, isochromosome, ring, inversion (paracentric/pericentric), duplication.
Robertsonian: fusion of two acrocentrics, 45 chromosomes, trisomy risk. Reciprocal: segment exchange between non-homologous chromosomes.
Karyotype 5-10 Mb; FISH 100 kb-1 Mb; CMA 10-50 kb; MLPA exon level; NGS nucleotide level.
CMA misses balanced rearrangements; NGS is limited for large structural anomalies.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:genetics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Mitotic chromosome. Fully condensed, about 10,000-fold compaction.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:genetics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: B-DNA. Right-handed double helix, about 2 nm wide, 10 bp per 3.4 nm turn.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:genetics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Chromatin states. Euchromatin: loose, accessible, active. Heterochromatin: dense, inactive, structural or regulatory.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:genetics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Looped domains. 300-nm fibre attached to a protein scaffold (topoisomerase II, SC2, lamins, cohesin).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:genetics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Nucleosome. About 146 bp wrapped twice around an octamer of two each of H2A, H2B, H3, H4: first level of compaction.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:genetics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Solenoid. 30-nm fibre of 6 nucleosomes per turn organised by H1; linker DNA about 55 bp; scaffold proteins.

title: Key historical figures of DNA structure?
subject: subj:genetics1

body.front: Key historical figures of DNA structure?
body.back: Watson and Crick (1953 model), Wilkins, Rosalind Franklin (X-ray Photo 51), Chargaff (base ratios).
A = T, G = C; (A+G)/(T+C) = 1; (G+C)/(A+T) varies between species.
A=T two hydrogen bonds; G≡C three hydrogen bonds.
B: right-handed, ~10 bp/turn, physiological. A: right-handed, ~11 bp, dehydrated/RNA-DNA hybrids. Z: left-handed, ~12 bp, rare.
~2 nm diameter; 10 bp per turn = 3.4 nm; 0.34 nm between nucleotides.
~3.055 billion bp; 1-5% coding (~20,000 genes); ~45% repeats (SINE, LINE, LTR).
Launched late 1980s; drafts 2001; completion 2003; T2T complete genome 2022.
Nucleosome 11 nm (146 bp + octamer), solenoid 30 nm (6 nucleosomes/turn, H1), loops 300 nm, chromatid 700 nm, mitotic chromosome.
Euchromatin: loose, accessible, active, acetylated. Heterochromatin: dense, inactive, deacetylated, methylated.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:genetics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Autosomal dominant. Every generation affected (vertical); Aa × aa gives 50% risk per pregnancy; watch for incomplete penetrance and de novo cases.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:genetics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Autosomal recessive. Affected siblings in one generation (horizontal); carrier parents Aa × Aa give 25% affected, 50% carriers; consanguinity raises risk.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:genetics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Mitochondrial. Maternal only; both sexes affected; heteroplasmy explains variable severity.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:genetics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: X-linked dominant. Both sexes; affected father transmits to all daughters and no sons; often more severe in males.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:genetics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: X-linked recessive. Mostly males; transmitted through carrier mothers; no father-to-son transmission; skips generations (grandfather → carrier daughter → grandson).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:genetics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Y-linked (holandric). Only males; father to every son (e.g. SRY, AZF spermatogenesis genes).

title: Genetic disease burden and Morocco's profile?
subject: subj:genetics1

body.front: Genetic disease burden and Morocco's profile?
body.back: 6-8% of births worldwide; in Morocco ~74% AR, 17% AD, 5% X-linked, 0.4% mitochondrial, 0.4% Y-linked.
Explain the disease and its cause, assess recurrence risk, discuss options (prenatal, preimplantation, presymptomatic diagnosis), support decisions.
Dominant: same phenotype hetero/homozygous. Incomplete: intermediate phenotype. Co-dominant: both expressed (ABO).
Vertical, both sexes, 50% risk; pitfalls: de novo, germline mosaicism, incomplete penetrance, variable expressivity, pleiotropy.
Achondroplasia (FGFR3), NF1, Marfan (FBN1), osteogenesis imperfecta, ADPKD, CMT1A, hereditary angioedema.
Horizontal, carrier parents, 25% affected, 50% carriers, consanguinity; CF, thalassaemia, albinism, Wilson, SMA, haemochromatosis.
Mostly males, no father-to-son transmission, carrier mothers, skipped generations; haemophilia A/B, DMD, colour blindness.
Both sexes; affected father → all daughters, no sons; often severe in males; fragile X, hypophosphataemic rickets.
Y-linked (father → sons), mitochondrial (maternal, heteroplasmy), multifactorial (liability threshold), imprinting (parent-of-origin expression).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:genetics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Nitrogenous bases. Purines (A, G) pair with pyrimidines (T/U, C): A-T/U, G-C, giving a uniform helix width.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:genetics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: N-glycosidic bond. Joins the sugar's C1′ to N1 of pyrimidines or N9 of purines.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:genetics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: DNA. Hereditary molecule in the nucleus and mitochondria; copied by replication.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:genetics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Phosphate group. Links sugars into the backbone and gives DNA its negative charge.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:genetics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Protein. Made by translation in the cytoplasm; determines the phenotype.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:genetics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: RNA. Intermediate molecule (mRNA, tRNA, rRNA) made by transcription.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:genetics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Pentose sugar. Links to phosphate and base; deoxyribose in DNA, ribose in RNA.
Genetics: study of genes, heredity and variation. Gene: DNA segment with instructions. Heredity: transmission to offspring. Variation: DNA differences between individuals.
DNA → (replication) DNA; DNA → (transcription) RNA; RNA → (translation) protein.
Phosphate group, pentose sugar (deoxyribose/ribose), nitrogenous base.
Purines A, G; pyrimidines C, T (DNA), U (RNA); A-T/U and G-C, uniform helix width.
Nucleoside: base + sugar (deoxyadenosine). Nucleotide: nucleoside + phosphate (dAMP, dATP).
Links the sugar's C1′ to N1 of pyrimidines or N9 of purines.
The 3′-OH of the chain bonds the 5′-phosphate of the next nucleotide: 3′-5′ phosphodiester bond; synthesis 5′→3′.
Thymine is uracil with a methyl group at C5; T in DNA, U in RNA.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:genetics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Frameshift. Insertion or deletion not multiple of 3 shifts the reading frame; e.g. Tay-Sachs (HEXA).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:genetics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Missense. Changes one amino acid; conservative or non-conservative. Sickle cell disease: HBB Glu→Val.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:genetics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Nonsense. Creates a stop codon: truncated, often degraded protein. Duchenne (DMD); β-thalassaemia codon 39 (Gln→stop).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:genetics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Readthrough. A stop codon becomes a sense codon, giving a C-terminally extended protein.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:genetics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Synonymous (silent). Uses code degeneracy, often the 3rd base; usually neutral, occasionally affects splicing or regulation (e.g. NOD2, Crohn's).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:genetics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Substitution. Transition: purine↔purine or pyrimidine↔pyrimidine (twice as common). Transversion: purine↔pyrimidine.

title: Define gene mutation and its frequency.
subject: subj:genetics1

body.front: Define gene mutation and its frequency.
body.back: Permanent DNA sequence change with a normal karyotype; 10⁻⁴-10⁻⁸ per gene per generation (~10⁻⁶), higher in large genes and at CpG hot spots.
Germline: in gametes, inherited, in all offspring cells. Somatic: in body cells, limited to the individual and the mutant clone.
Coexistence of cells with different genotypes in one individual: somatic (early embryo) or germline (gonads).
Transition: purine↔purine or pyrimidine↔pyrimidine (≈2× more common). Transversion: purine↔pyrimidine.
SNV/SNP (> 1%), STR (1-4 nt), VNTR (10-60 nt), CNV (copy number).
Silent (NOD2), missense (sickle cell HBB Glu→Val), nonsense (DMD; β-thal codon 39), readthrough (extended protein).
Exon: truncated/dominant-negative protein. Promoter: altered expression. Splice site: exon skipping, intron retention. 3′ UTR: mRNA instability.
Loss-of-function, gain-of-function, hypomorphic, hypermorphic, conditional, lethal, dominant-negative, neutral.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:genetics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Helicase. ATP-dependent unwinding that breaks base-pair hydrogen bonds and opens the fork (MCM, part of the CMG complex).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:genetics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Lagging strand. Made discontinuously away from the fork as Okazaki fragments by Pol δ.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:genetics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Leading strand. Synthesised continuously toward the fork by Pol ε, needing only one primer.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:genetics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Ligation. DNA ligase I joins Okazaki fragments into a continuous strand.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:genetics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: PCNA. Sliding clamp loaded by replication factor C; boosts processivity.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:genetics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Primase-Pol α. Lays down short RNA-DNA primers (10-20 nt); Pol α has no proofreading.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:genetics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Primer removal. RNase H and FEN1 remove RNA primers; Pol δ fills the gaps.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:genetics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: RPA (SSB). Single-strand binding protein that stabilises unwound DNA, prevents reannealing and protects from nucleases.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:genetics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Topoisomerase. Type I cuts one strand (no ATP); type II cuts both (ATP; gyrase in bacteria) to relieve supercoiling.
Each new DNA molecule has one parental and one new strand (Meselson-Stahl).
DNA template, DNA polymerases, replication proteins, dNTPs, ATP, Mg²⁺.
Prokaryotes: one origin per chromosome. Eukaryotes: many, ~40 kb apart, recognised by ORC, licensed once per cycle, bidirectional forks.

title: Roles of helicase, RPA and topoisomerases?
subject: subj:genetics1

body.front: Roles of helicase, RPA and topoisomerases?
body.back: Helicase unwinds (ATP). RPA stabilises ssDNA. Topo I cuts one strand (no ATP); topo II cuts both (ATP) to relieve supercoiling.
α: priming, no proofreading. δ: lagging. ε: leading. β: repair. γ: mitochondrial.
Leading: continuous toward the fork, one primer, Pol ε. Lagging: Okazaki fragments away from the fork, many primers, Pol δ, ligase I.
RNase H + FEN1 remove primers; Pol δ fills gaps; DNA ligase I seals.
Removing the last primer leaves a gap so telomeres shorten; telomerase adds TTAGGG repeats.

title: E. coli vs eukaryotic replication machinery?
subject: subj:genetics1

body.front: E. coli vs eukaryotic replication machinery?
body.back: Pol III vs Pol δ/ε; Pol I vs RNase H/FEN1; DnaB vs CMG; SSB vs RPA; DnaG vs primase-Pol α; β-clamp vs PCNA.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:genetics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: 5′ capping. Added at ~20-30 nt: triphosphatase, guanylyltransferase, methyltransferase give m⁷G; protects, exports, starts translation.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:genetics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: RNA editing. Individual bases are chemically changed after transcription, e.g. A→I in glutamate receptor mRNA.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:genetics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Export. Only fully processed mRNA leaves the nucleus; faulty RNAs are degraded.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:genetics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Polyadenylation. CPSF binds AAUAAA, CstF binds the GU-rich region; cleavage then poly(A) polymerase adds ~200 A; PABP binds.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:genetics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Primary transcript. Pre-mRNA with no cap, no tail and all introns.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:genetics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Splicing. Spliceosome of snRNPs removes introns by two transesterifications, forming a lariat, and joins exons.
5′ capping, polyadenylation, splicing, RNA editing, nuclear export.
m⁷G via 5′-5′ triphosphate; triphosphatase, guanylyltransferase, methyltransferase; protects, exports, starts translation, helps first-intron splicing.
CPSF (AAUAAA), CstF (GU-rich), CFIm/CFIIm cleave; poly(A) polymerase adds ~200 A; PABP stabilises.
snRNAs + proteins forming snRNPs U1, U2, U4/U6, U5; recognise 5′ site, 3′ site, branch point.
Two transesterifications: branch-point A 2′-OH attacks 5′ site (lariat); exon 3′-OH attacks 3′ site (exons joined).
Exon skipping, alternative 5′/3′ sites, intron retention, mutually exclusive exons; regulated by SR proteins and hnRNPs.
Fibronectin, calcitonin/CGRP, tropomyosin, Bcl-xL/Bcl-xS, CD44, Dscam, SMN1/SMN2.
Editing: single bases changed (A→I by ADAR, C→U by APOBEC). Splicing: exon combinations change.
Prokaryotes: no introns, no cap, rare poly(A), cytoplasm, coupled translation. Eukaryotes: all processing, nucleus, separate translation.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:genetics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Promoter clearance. TFIIH kinase phosphorylates the Pol II CTD, which changes shape and leaves the promoter to elongate.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:genetics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: TFIIF + Pol II. TFIIF escorts RNA Pol II to the promoter and stabilises its binding.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:genetics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: TATA box. Core promoter element about 25-30 bp upstream of +1; other elements: Inr at +1, DPE at +28 to +32, CAAT and GC boxes.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:genetics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: TFIIB. Bridges TFIID and Pol II, positioning the polymerase at the +1 start site.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:genetics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: TFIID. First factor to bind; its TBP subunit recognises the TATA box and bends DNA; with 13 TAFs; TFIIA stabilises it.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:genetics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: TFIIE and TFIIH. TFIIE recruits TFIIH, completing the PIC; TFIIH helicase unwinds DNA (ATP) to form the open complex.
Hydrogen bonds (A-T 2, G-C 3), base stacking (hydrophobic), electrostatic interactions with ions.
Temperature at which 50% of base pairs separate; increased by GC content, length and cation concentration.
Template (antisense) is read 3′→5′; sense (coding) has the same sequence as mRNA (T→U).
Pol I: 28S, 18S, 5.8S rRNA (nucleolus). Pol II: mRNA, snRNA, lncRNA. Pol III: tRNA, 5S rRNA, U6, 7SL.

title: What is the Pol II CTD?
subject: subj:genetics1

body.front: What is the Pol II CTD?
body.back: C-terminal repeats of YSPTSPS (52 in humans) on RPB1; phosphorylation coordinates capping, splicing, polyadenylation and phase transitions.
TATA box (−25/−30, TBP), Inr (+1), DPE (+28/+32), CAAT box (CTF), GC box (Sp1).

title: Roles of the general transcription factors?
subject: subj:genetics1

body.front: Roles of the general transcription factors?
body.back: TFIID: binds TATA (TBP). TFIIA: stabilises. TFIIB: positions Pol II. TFIIF: escorts Pol II. TFIIE: recruits TFIIH. TFIIH: helicase + CTD kinase.
Activators: enhancers, coactivators, HATs, more Pol II. Repressors: silencers, corepressors, HDACs, less Pol II.
AAUAAA → CPSF + CstF cleave → poly(A) polymerase adds tail → XRN2 degrades the remaining RNA → Pol II released.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:genetics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: A site. Aminoacyl site: the charged tRNA arrives as eEF1A-GTP-aa-tRNA; correct pairing triggers GTP hydrolysis (fidelity checkpoint).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:genetics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: E site. Exit site: the deacylated tRNA leaves.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:genetics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: P site. Peptidyl site: holds the tRNA carrying the growing chain; the initiator Met-tRNAi starts here.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:genetics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Peptidyl transferase. The A-site amino group attacks the P-site ester bond; the chain moves onto the A-site tRNA. Catalysed by rRNA.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:genetics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Termination. eRF1 recognises UAA, UAG, UGA; its GGQ motif releases the peptide; eRF3-GTP escorts it; ribosome recycled.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:genetics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Translocation. eEF2-GTP moves the ribosome 3 nucleotides: A→P, P→E.
Triplet, universal (exceptions: mitochondria, ciliates), degenerate, non-overlapping, with stop codons; 64 codons for 20 amino acids.
Mitochondria: UGA = Trp, AUA = Met. Ciliates: UAA, UAG = Gln.
Free: cytosolic, nuclear, mitochondrial proteins. ER-bound: secreted and membrane proteins, targeted by SRP.
ORF: continuous codons from start to stop. Frameshift: 1-2 nt insertion/deletion changes all downstream codons (CF, Tay-Sachs).
70-95 nt; cloverleaf with DHU loop, anticodon loop, TΨC loop, CCA 3′ end; L-shaped in 3D; modified bases.
Charge each tRNA with its amino acid: aa + ATP → aminoacyl-adenylate → transfer to tRNA 3′ end.
80S = 40S (decoding) + 60S (peptidyl transferase rRNA); ~60% rRNA; A, P, E sites.
Flexible pairing at the codon's 3rd base (e.g. G-U), letting one tRNA read several codons.
43S (40S + eIF1/1A/3/5 + eIF2-GTP-Met-tRNAi) → eIF4E/4G/4A bind cap → 48S scans to AUG (Kozak) → eIF2 GTP hydrolysis → eIF5B joins 60S → 80S.
eEF1A-GTP delivers aa-tRNA to A site → peptidyl transfer → eEF2-GTP translocation (A→P, P→E).
Stop codon (UAA/UAG/UGA) → eRF1 (GGQ) with eRF3-GTP releases peptide → Rli1 recycles subunits.
